name: Kidney failure risk
seoTitle: Kidney failure risk Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Kidney failure risk: work out albumin-to-creatinine ratio from the age and the EGFR. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the age, the EGFR, the albumin and the bicarbonate and the Kidney failure risk calculator solves for albumin-to-creatinine ratio. It is built for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Kidney failure risk calculator work?
sections.html:
The Kidney failure risk calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports albumin-to-creatinine ratio in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex); then you type in the age, the EGFR, the albumin and the bicarbonate.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A number, expressed in years.
  • A number, expressed in mL/min/1.73m².
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milliequivalents per liter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in Mg/d l.
  • A number, expressed in pts.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Kidney failure risk calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Albumin-to-creatinine ratio=-sex + kidney failure risk score − (age) − (albumin) − (bicarbonate) − (calcium) − (EGFR) − (phosphorus)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Albumin units, opening in grams per deciliter
  • Winters, Na_K, opening in milliequivalents per liter
  • Calcium level, opening in milligrams per deciliter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Kidney failure risk calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the age, the EGFR and the albumin — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Kidney failure risk calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns albumin-to-creatinine ratio, derived from the age, the EGFR and the albumin. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Kidney failure risk calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, the EGFR, the albumin and the bicarbonate, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter albumin in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Albumin opens in grams per deciliter and the chip beside it offers 2 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Kidney failure risk calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
